◆ Warm-up · Verdict
››
03 / 56
Verdict

A myth
about an error.

No decimal slip has ever been found in the sources. The “decimal” story itself spread through citations nobody checked.

  • Early iron values were high for other reasons: contaminated samples and fresh vs dried confusion.
  • Popeye’s creator credited spinach for vitamin A in 1932, not iron.
  • The decimal tale was repeated in the BMJ (1981) and copied from there, again and again.

Fluent + plausible + repeated = “known fact”. That is also how an AI hallucination travels from a chatbot into a poster.

Sutton, M. (2010). Spinach, iron and Popeye: Ironic lessons from biochemical history and the importance of healthy scepticism. Internet Journal of Criminology. Rekdal, O. B. (2014). Academic urban legends. Social Studies of Science, 44(4), 638–654. Schwarcz, J., “Spinach and iron”, McGill Office for Science and Society.
The twist: people who “debunk” the spinach myth with the decimal story are spreading a second myth. Rekdal (2014) uses it as the classic academic urban legend. Rule for today: check the source, not the story.

Dulu vs Kini · clinical nutrition’s first trial

1747: good evidence, weak persuasion

  • James Lind’s citrus pair recovered within days. One was fit for duty in six.
  • He published six years later, inside A Treatise of the Scurvy, tentatively and without pressing the case.
  • The Navy issued daily lemon juice in 1795: about 48 years after the trial.

Kini: evidence that is not communicated well changes nothing. AI can help you be read, but only if the evidence underneath is right.

Liang, W., Yuksekgonul, M., Mao, Y., Wu, E., & Zou, J. (2023). GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers. Patterns, 4(7), 100779.
Lind, J. (1753). A Treatise of the Scurvy. Edinburgh. “The mysteries of James Lind and scurvy”, Hektoen International (2017). Historians also blame cost and Admiralty inertia, not only Lind.
◆ Block 1 · Dulu vs Kini
››
11 / 56
Dulu vs Kini · plain-language health writing

9th–11th century: medicine for people without a doctor

  • al-Rāzī wrote Man lā yaḥḍuruhu al-ṭabīb, “For one who has no physician”: a self-help manual using cheap, easy-to-find remedies.
  • Ibn Sīnā condensed medicine into a teaching poem of about 1,326 verses, the Urjūza fī al-ṭibb, so students could memorise it.
  • Same knowledge, different reader, different form.

Kini: a plain-language summary and a patient leaflet are the same idea. AI makes the rewrite fast; checking it is still the physician’s duty.

US National Library of Medicine, Islamic Medical Manuscripts: “Monographs” (al-Rāzī) and “Poetry” (Ibn Sīnā’s Urjūza, usually 1,326 verses). Image: “Avicenna canon 1597”, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
Optional if short on time. Connects to the patient-leaflet demo in Block 3.

◆ Block 1 · The one rule
››
14 / 56

The one rule for today

DELEGATE · TASKS

  • grammar, clarity, word count
  • reformatting for a new audience
  • first-draft translation you verify
  • layout and chart code you audit
  • predicting audience questions

KEEP · JUDGMENT

  • the finding and its size
  • the uncertainty: CIs, limits, hedges
  • the clinical recommendation
  • who the reader is and what they need
  • every citation and every number

Delegate tasks. Never delegate judgment.

The right column is what a reviewer, an examiner and a patient all rely on.

  • Two answers contradicted guidelines (snacking in obesity; supplements in NAFLD).
  • Key recommendations were missing; CKD protein advice ignored the stage.

Plausible and incomplete is the hardest error to see, for patients and for authors.

Older model, yes; but the failure mode (fluent, partly right, quietly incomplete) is the one to train your eye on.

What can chloride be replaced with?

Chloride can often be substituted with other halides, such as bromide, depending on the application. Context matters.

No health warning. No question about why you are asking.

The doctors’ own re-test with ChatGPT-3.5, paraphrased

Evidence 2 · Annals of Internal Medicine: Clinical Cases, Aug 2025

The salt swap that ended in psychosis

  • A 60-year-old man who had studied nutrition wanted to cut chloride from his diet.
  • After consulting ChatGPT, he replaced table salt with sodium bromide for 3 months.
  • Paranoia, hallucinations, an involuntary psychiatric hold: bromism, a 19th-century diagnosis.

The answer was true in a cleaning-chemistry context. In a diet context it was poison. Context is part of the message.

Eichenberger, A., Thielke, S., & Van Buskirk, A. (2025). A case of bromism influenced by use of artificial intelligence. Annals of Internal Medicine: Clinical Cases. doi:10.7326/aimcc.2024.1260. Emulated chat reconstructs the authors’ description; the patient’s own log was unavailable.
Authors could not see his actual chat; their re-test produced bromide with no warning. Use it to ask: when you write for the public, what context does your sentence carry with it?

◆ Block 2 · What journals allow
››
19 / 56

What journals and UKM allow in 2026

Allowed
  • Language, clarity and readability
  • Organising your own content
  • Literature search support
  • Plain grammar checks (no declaration needed at Elsevier)
Allowed if declared
  • Substantive rewording or restructuring
  • Translation
  • AI in data analysis or figures: Methods
  • AI in writing: declaration / acknowledgments
Never
  • AI as an author
  • AI-written core content passed off as yours
  • Unverified references
  • Uploading a manuscript you are reviewing

Always read the target journal’s policy page before you submit. Image rules are usually the strictest.

Elsevier, Generative AI policies for journals (updated June 2026). ICMJE Recommendations, current version, sections on AI-assisted technology (icmje.org). UKM Guideline (2025), §2.2.
Clinical Nutrition, Clinical Nutrition ESPEN and AJCN are Elsevier journals; Nutrients (MDPI) has its own page. The common core is the same.

Critique, not write: Nurul’s discussion

draft · Discussion ¶1
EMULATED

This trial proves that the Pinggan Sihat plan reverses type 2 diabetes. HbA1c fell by 0.4%, which is clinically important. These results agree with previous studies on low-GI diets. Malaysian clinics should adopt this plan for all patients.

Results table: 8.2% → 7.8% · −0.4 percentage points (95% CI −0.7 to −0.1) · single centre · 12 weeks

🔒 gemini · UKM account
EMULATED
✦

1. “proves” — one RCT cannot prove; suggest “suggests” or “indicates”.

2. “reverses” — 7.8% is still above most targets; no remission was measured.

3. “0.4%” — ambiguous: percentage points or relative? Add mmol/mol.

4. “previous studies” — no citations; which studies, what effect sizes?

5. “all patients” — one clinic, 12 weeks; generalisability not shown.

I have not rewritten your text.

◆ Block 2 · Hedge drift

››
25 / 56
The quiet risk in “just fix my English”

Hedge drift: when polishing changes the science

NURUL’S SENTENCE

Higher fibre intake was associated with lower HbA1c, and the plan may help some patients improve glycaemic control.

“POLISHED” BY AN AI TOOL

Higher fibre intake was associated with reduces HbA1c, and the plan may help some helps patients improve achieve glycaemic control.

Association → cause · “linked to” becomes “reduces”

Some → all · qualifiers quietly vanish

Improve → achieve · a modest effect becomes a target met

Prompt: “Edit grammar only. Keep every hedge, number and unit. Show changes.” Then compare line by line (Word: Compare documents).

Illustrative example constructed for teaching.
Show the tracked changes. These three edits would each be flagged by a reviewer, and none looks like a mistake at a glance.
◆ Block 2 · Context, not magic words
››
26 / 56
TASK Critique my discussion against my results.
CONTEXT MSc clinical nutrition; RCT, n=120, T2DM; journal: Clinical Nutrition ESPEN.
SOURCES [results table] [my paragraph] [CONSORT 2025]
CONSTRAINTS Don’t rewrite. Don’t add references. Keep numbers, units and hedges.
FORMAT Numbered list: sentence → problem → why.
CHECK Say “unsure” rather than guess.

From prompting to context

  • Personas (“act as a professor of dietetics…”) matter less than real sources.
  • Constraints protect the meaning: numbers, units, hedges.
  • Asking for “unsure” makes errors visible instead of silent.
Copy this structure. It works in Gemini, NotebookLM, or any tool.

◆ Block 2 · Five checks
››
28 / 56

Five checks for every AI-surfaced citation

1

Exists

DOI resolves; found in PubMed, Scopus or the publisher site.

2

Matches

Authors, year, title, journal all correct. No “Frankenstein” mixes.

3

Read

You read the relevant part, not just the abstract.

4

Supports

It says what you cite it for: same population, same outcome.

5

Standing

Not retracted (publisher page, Retraction Watch).

UKM rule: never include a citation you have not personally checked against the original. In nutrition, check #4 hardest: a rat study cited for a human claim is a common slip.

UKM Guideline (2025), §2.3: Accuracy, bias, fabricated references and integrity risks.

◆ Block 3 · Dulu vs Kini
››
32 / 56
Dulu vs Kini · figures that changed policy

A picture can win the argument

  • John Snow mapped cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump: the cluster made the case.
  • Florence Nightingale’s “rose” showed that far more soldiers died of preventable disease (blue) than of wounds (red).
  • Neither had software. Both chose one comparison that mattered.

Kini: AI draws a chart in seconds. Choosing which comparison deserves the picture is still your job.

Snow, J. (1855). On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (2nd ed.). Image: “Snow-cholera-map-1”, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (cropped). Nightingale, F. (1858). Notes on Matters Affecting the Health, Efficiency, and Hospital Administration of the British Army. London: Harrison. Rose redrawn schematically for this slide; wedge sizes are illustrative, not her data.
Snow: epidemiology. Nightingale: statistics as persuasion, which led to sanitation reform. Ask: what single comparison in your project deserves a figure?
◆ Block 3 · Figure rules
››
33 / 56

AI and figures: four rules (Elsevier, June 2026)

ALLOWED · DECLARE IN CAPTION

Explanatory images

Flow charts, study schematics, timelines.

e.g. CONSORT-style flow diagram layout

ONLY IF REPRODUCIBLE

Data charts

Plots must come straight from your data, by a method in Methods.

e.g. code you ran on your dataset

NEVER CREATE OR ALTER

Primary images

Microscopy, radiology, patient photos.

e.g. food photos for intake, DXA, ultrasound

NO GENERAL IMAGE AI

Graphical abstracts

Use dedicated scientific illustration tools instead.

e.g. BioRender, your own drawing

Nutrition-specific trap: food photographs used to estimate intake are research data. Never “enhance” them with AI.

Elsevier, Generative AI policies for journals (updated June 2026): images, graphical abstracts and cover art.
Journals differ; Elsevier’s June 2026 policy is the clearest and most clinical nutrition journals follow something similar. Cover art is a separate case needing editor permission.
◆ Block 3 · Integrity case
››
34 / 56
Figure 1 · labels as published
RECONSTRUCTED
Integrity case · February 2024

The figure nobody read

  • A review in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology used Midjourney figures, declared in the paper.
  • Labels were gibberish: “testtomcels”, “Dissisilcied”, “dck”. An anatomically absurd rat went viral.
  • It passed peer review and was retracted within days of publication.

Declaring AI use is necessary, not sufficient. Read every label, every axis, every unit.

Reported in Popular Science, “A ridiculous AI-generated rat penis made it into a peer-reviewed journal” (Feb 2024); Frontiers retraction notice (2024). Figure reconstructed schematically with the reported labels; not the original image.
Do not show the original image; the labels make the point. Reviewers and editors missed it too: responsibility stays with the authors.

Talk · 10 minutes + Q&A

AI as a rehearsal partner

  • Hard questions, grounded in your paper, before the real audience asks them.
  • Timing: about 130 words a minute; ask it to cut your script to 1,300 words.
  • Audio Overview: hear two AI hosts discuss your paper. What they stress is what a listener takes away.

You still give the talk. Answers you only read from AI will not survive a follow-up question.

Emulated interface. NotebookLM features: Audio Overviews, Video Overviews, and (since late 2025) Slide Decks and Infographics; Google, “8 ways to make the most out of Slide Decks in NotebookLM” (Dec 2025).

Good as a draft

  • A first storyboard for your talk

Not a deliverable until checked

  • Every number, unit and arrow on every frame
  • Generated pictures of food, organs, people

NotebookLM (UKM account) offers Audio and Video Overviews, Slide Decks and Infographics. Treat them as a mirror of your writing, not as finished outputs.

Writing for the public

Same number, two headlines

Relative · sounds big

“Blood sugar cut by 5%”

0.4 ÷ 8.2 ≈ 5%. Correct arithmetic, misleading impression.

Absolute · honest

“HbA1c 8.2% → 7.8%”

A small drop; most participants still above target.

1 finding

1 absolute number

1 limitation

1 link to the paper

Prompt any caption with: “Use absolute numbers. Keep the limitation. No cure words.”

Fictional numbers from the worked example.
Relative framing is the oldest trick in health news. AI picks whichever framing sounds most engaging unless you constrain it.

◆ Block 4 · Data safety
››
45 / 56

What never goes into a public AI tool

👤

Patients

Diet records, food photos, lab results, case notes, interview recordings, even “de-identified” small samples.

📄

Unpublished work

Manuscripts, theses, grant proposals, and anything you are asked to review.

🏥

Institutional

Hospital protocols, internal reports, data under an ethics or data-sharing agreement.

Health data is sensitive personal data under Malaysia’s PDPA 2010. Unsure? UKM’s default: don’t upload. Use synthetic data to test prompts.

Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (Act 709), as amended 2024. UKM Guideline (2025), §2.3: Data security, confidentiality and privacy.
Your ethics approval and consent forms almost certainly do not cover uploading data to a chatbot. Use your UKM account for published material only.

Reviewers must never upload a manuscript into an AI tool. They may use a private tool to polish their own words, and must declare it.

◆ Block 4 · AI detectors
››
47 / 56

About AI detectors

  • Scores are probabilistic. False positives happen, more often for non-native English writers.
  • UKM won’t decide misconduct on a score alone.
  • Concerns go to academic judgment and an oral check of your understanding.

Your best protection

Drafts, version history, notes, analysis code, an AI-use log, and a clear declaration.

“No adverse academic decision shall be made solely on algorithmic inference.”

UKM Guideline (2025), §2.3: Use of AI-detection tools (e.g., Turnitin, ZeroGPT, GPTZero). Liang, W., et al. (2023). GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers. Patterns, 4(7), 100779.

◆ Wrap-up
››
51 / 56

Six things to remember

01

Carry the message, keep the meaning.

Size and certainty survive every rewrite.

02

Structure before style.

Your reporting guideline is the outline.

03

Critique, don’t write.

You draft; AI finds the gaps.

04

Every number, citation and label is yours.

Check them; nobody else will.

05

Patients get plain, warm, tested words.

Absolute numbers, no cure words, teach-back.

06

Never upload what you must protect. Declare the rest.

PDPA, UKM levels, journal policy, AI-use log.

◆ Closing · History rhymes
››
53 / 56
Closing · every generation fears its new tool

We have been here before

c. 370 BCE

WRITING · PLATO, PHAEDRUS

“[T]his invention will produce forgetfulness in the minds of those who learn to use it… the appearance of wisdom, not true wisdom.”

King Thamus, judging the invention of writing

1986

CALCULATORS · WASHINGTON, D.C.

Mathematics teachers picketed the NCTM meeting over calculators in classrooms. Textbook author John Saxon warned of “a tremendous potential for destruction” of students’ skills.

2026

GENERATIVE AI · THIS ROOM

“Will AI make us stop writing, and stop thinking?”

The case report, the rat and the citation audit say the risk is real, if we stop checking.

Plato, Phaedrus 275a, trans. H. N. Fowler (1914), Loeb Classical Library (public domain). “The great calculator debate”, The Christian Science Monitor, 9 May 1986.
Read the Phaedrus line slowly. Ask: were they wrong?
◆ Closing · Were they wrong?
››
54 / 56
Closing · were they wrong?

Right about the risk. Wrong about the ending.

Writing

Memory did change. Writing also gave us journals, case reports, leaflets: everything in today’s lecture.

Calculators

Mental arithmetic did weaken. We still teach it first, then hand over the calculator, and expect you to notice a wrong answer.

Learn to say it yourself. Then delegate the wording. Always know when the meaning changed.

P.S. The only reason we know Socrates distrusted writing is that Plato wrote it down.

Pause before the P.S. Then thank you and questions.
